concepts.decision: Specify data state, adversary, mechanism, keys, endpoint behavior, recovery, and monitoring.
concepts.definition: Use of cryptographic mechanisms within a complete system of keys, protocols, trust, and operations.
concepts.failureExample: Encryption is deployed while access control and key export remain uncontrolled.
concepts.label: Cryptography

concepts.decision: Use when secure shared-key handling can be provided.
concepts.definition: Shared-key method suited to efficient bulk data protection.
concepts.failureExample: A high-volume dataset uses public-key encryption alone without a workable performance or key plan.
concepts.label: Symmetric Cryptography

concepts.decision: Use when public verification or scalable keying is required.
concepts.definition: Public/private-key method for exchange, signatures, and trust distribution.
concepts.failureExample: A system trusts a public key whose owner was never authenticated.
concepts.label: Asymmetric Cryptography

concepts.decision: Use with a trusted expected value or authenticated construction.
concepts.definition: Fixed-length digest used for integrity-related verification.
concepts.failureExample: A plaintext hash is described as encryption.
concepts.label: Hash

concepts.decision: Use when third parties need to validate a signed object.
concepts.definition: Evidence mechanism for origin and integrity under a private key and validation context.
concepts.failureExample: A code signature is accepted without checking certificate validity or revocation status.
concepts.label: Digital Signature

concepts.decision: Use when managed certificate trust is required across parties or services.
concepts.definition: Operational system for identity-to-public-key binding, issuance, validation, and revocation.
concepts.failureExample: A certificate is trusted solely because it contains a signature.
concepts.label: Public Key Infrastructure

concepts.decision: Design it alongside any cryptographic mechanism before relying on the mechanism.
concepts.definition: Controls for key creation, custody, access, use, rotation, recovery, and destruction.
concepts.failureExample: A service owner can export all production private keys without approval.
concepts.label: Key Management

concepts.decision: Define authority, evidence, and compromise handling for each transition.
concepts.definition: Lifecycle transitions for keys from generation to destruction or archival.
concepts.failureExample: A certificate expires but its dependent service and owners are unknown.
concepts.label: Key Lifecycle

concepts.decision: Validate issuer, trust anchor, identity/name, validity, intended use, and status.
concepts.definition: Signed assertion binding an identity or service to a public key and associated constraints.
concepts.failureExample: A name-mismatched certificate is accepted because the chain is cryptographically valid.
concepts.label: Certificate

concepts.decision: Choose for its defined keying or signing role under policy.
concepts.definition: Asymmetric technique family requiring approved parameters and correct protocol integration.
concepts.failureExample: A team selects ECC but implements insecure custom protocol composition.
concepts.label: Elliptic Curve Cryptography

concepts.decision: Inventory uses and test governed replacement profiles before deployment.
concepts.definition: Migration consideration for relevant long-lived public-key protections.
concepts.failureExample: A procurement claim triggers untested protocol-wide replacement.
concepts.label: Post Quantum Cryptography

concepts.decision: Evaluate against actual link, endpoint, lifecycle, and assurance needs.
concepts.definition: Specialized key-establishment technology with physical and operational dependencies.
concepts.failureExample: QKD is proposed to compensate for unpatched endpoints.
concepts.label: Quantum Key Distribution

misconceptions.claim: Using encryption means data is secure.
misconceptions.correction: Protection depends on keys, endpoints, algorithms, protocols, configuration, identities, recovery, and operational handling.

outcome: Recommend a cryptographic solution direction for a protection requirement and identify the key-management or protocol dependency that could invalidate it.

sections.body: Symmetric cryptography is efficient for bulk data protection and requires secure shared-key handling. Asymmetric cryptography supports key exchange, signatures, and scalable trust patterns but has different performance and operational costs. Hashes support integrity checks but do not provide secrecy. Digital signatures support origin and integrity evidence under a managed key and certificate context. PKI manages identity-to-key bindings through issuance, validation, revocation, and lifecycle processes.
keyPoints: A primitive’s property is not the same as an end-to-end protocol guarantee.
Certificates and keys require lifecycle management, not just generation.
sections.title: Choose the right cryptographic role

sections.body: Key generation, storage, distribution, access, rotation, backup, recovery, revocation, escrow decisions, and destruction are security decisions. Protocol configuration must address authentication, freshness, downgrade resistance, parameter validation, and error handling. Emerging quantum concerns affect algorithm longevity and migration planning; they do not justify unsupported claims that every current system needs immediate replacement.
keyPoints: Loss or compromise of key material can defeat strong algorithms.
Cryptographic agility allows justified migration without uncontrolled change.
